claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2025-11 reports: The CCDR records over 152 deaths and US$1.2 billion in losses from hazards over decades; landslides led to dozens of villages abandoned or displaced in 40 years. Shovi’s 2023 debris flow in Racha killed at least 32 and affected over 200.

claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2025-11 reports: Among 100-year-flood-exposed people, 12% are poor and 77% have multiple vulnerabilities; among drought-exposed people, 12.1% are poor and 80% have multiple vulnerabilities. Kakheti is most drought-exposed; 91% there face other vulnerabilities.

claim_decisions.statement: The 2025 CCDR models higher food-price-related poverty under a dry/hot scenario than under stated policies, with particularly adverse consumption effects in Imereti, Mtskheta-Mtianeti, Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti and Kakheti. These are scenario results, not observed poverty changes.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: The text uses regional percentages alongside national percentage-point changes; precise regional magnitudes are omitted to avoid conflating these measures.

claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2025 reports: The UN analysis places spatial, social, political (including unresolved conflict) and environmental (including climate) factors among intersecting sources of vulnerability. Conflict disproportionately affects forcibly displaced people, residents outside government control and communities near Abkhazia/South Ossetia ABLs.
claim_decisions.uncertainty: Intersectional country-analysis framing; neither a climate-conflict causal estimate nor a local hazard assessment along administrative boundary lines.

claim_decisions.statement: Source dated 2020-11 reports: The 2020 assessment says historic wetland drainage worsens lowland flood risk and is linked to coastal erosion, particularly around Poti; dams and port works also disrupt sediment delivery, including from Khobistskali, contributing to erosion and sediment accumulation at Poti port.

pathways.climate_pressure: Flooding, drought and geological hazards in the source's regional climate-risk assessment.
pathways.documented_impact: Climate impacts threaten displaced households' safety and economic stability.
pathways.fcv_mediator: Protracted conflict-related displacement, inadequate housing and limited services and livelihood opportunities increase vulnerability.
pathways.possible_consequence: Displaced households may sustain greater hazard-related harm and livelihood disruption; no new violent conflict is inferred.
alternative_explanations: Poverty, building quality and hazard exposure also shape losses independently of displacement.
Regional synthesis is not a matched local comparison.
pathways.uncertainty: Source-stated vulnerability mechanism, not causal identification; do not assign uniform exposure to all IDPs or named conflict territories.
resilience_factors: Adequate housing, accessible basic services and livelihood support can reduce the stated vulnerability; effectiveness is not evaluated here.
pathways.compact_statement: Conflict-related displacement and inadequate housing/services can magnify climate-hazard vulnerability in Georgia; no climate-caused conflict claim.

gaps: The water-use conflict projection names no tested institutional mediator or observed local dispute; no complete pathway is inferred from that warning.
The reverse pathway concerns conflict-related displacement and vulnerability, not demonstrated interruption of a particular adaptation project.

executive_assessment.text: Named examples distinguish Shovi/Racha debris-flow impacts, drought-sensitive Kakheti, modeled regional poverty effects and human alterations to Poti's coastal sediment system.

Conflict-related displacement can deepen climate vulnerability through inadequate housing, restricted services and livelihood opportunities. This is a bounded reverse pathway, not evidence that climate caused Georgia's conflicts.
Reported municipal plans, basin mapping and monitoring systems are capacities and implementation outputs, not evaluated resilience or peace outcomes.
